extracted.intended_audience: public relations professionals, communications writers, and anyone drafting press release quotes (PR managers, corporate communications, agencies)
extracted.subtask_description: Best-practice guidance for crafting executive and other quotes to include in press releases so they are newsworthy, concise, and usable by reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length and Structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for one sentence, at most two; average length of quotes in major publications (NYT) is 19-20 words; maximum three sentences from any one speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep quotes short and tightly structured so they are easy for journalists to lift verbatim; avoid long multi-sentence statements and limit any single speaker to no more than three sentences in a release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid boilerplate and generic phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: "We're pleased to announce..." or "happy to support" statements; generic statements devoid of emotion; industry jargon and clichés (paradigm shift, pivot, synergy); adjectives that don't add information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are anti-patterns—such lines are unlikely to be picked up by reporters or to add news value. Replace generic praise with specific, insight-driven language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add Value and Insight
rubrics_metrics.description: A quote likely to be picked up should be: concise, compelling, fact-based, and make a point not made elsewhere in the release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the quote to add new information or perspective (not repeat the lead). Aim for a single memorable idea that advances the story and gives reporters something they couldn't otherwise paraphrase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on Impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus less on yourself, more on who/what you're impacting; skip quotes highlighting leadership's excitement; provide perspective the reporter could not generate themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame quotes around outcomes, customers, communities, or broader implications rather than internal celebration. Reporters favor quotes that illuminate effect and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound Natural
rubrics_metrics.description: Speak the language of the audience; conversational tone; avoid machine-generated feel; should sound like the person actually talks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write quotes that reflect a real voice—use natural phrasing and cadence. Avoid stilted, overly corporate, or legalistic language that reads as 'approved by legal' or AI-generated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote Placement
rubrics_metrics.description: CEO or key leader should be quoted; place at the third or fourth paragraph; not the second paragraph (lead should be facts, not quotes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use placement strategically: open with factual lead, then follow with a high-value quote around paragraph three or four to add context and human perspective without overshadowing the facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper Attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: After the quote: speaker's full name, title, organization; use "said" (AP style); format example: "Quote here," said John Smith, CEO of Acme Corp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow AP-style attribution and include full identifying information immediately after the quote so reporters can attribute correctly and use the quote without additional verification steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-Person Quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: If using two quotes, they should make different points; often: one from internal leader (CEO), one from external party (customer, partner, expert); external quote adds credibility and outside perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When including two voices, ensure they complement each other—one can provide organizational context, the other independent validation or real-world impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit Rubric for Newsworthy Quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Says something that wouldn't be said in marketing copy; provides insight only that person could provide; has personality; could conceivably be quoted in a news article; doesn't sound like it was "approved by legal".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist as a final filter: if the line sounds like marketing spin or legal-approved boilerplate, rewrite it to be specific, personal, and newsworthy so journalists will treat it as usable color or attribution.
